compressed_text: Volkswagen announced on September 26, 2025, that it will pause production for one week in early October at its Zwickau and Dresden electric vehicle plants in eastern Germany, citing adaptation to market conditions. Bloomberg also reported temporary shutdowns at an EV plant in Emden, though VW did not confirm. The move reflects weak European EV demand due to high upfront costs and limited charging infrastructure. The Zwickau and Dresden sites produce VW’s ID. family of EVs and Audi’s Q4 e-tron. This follows Bosch cutting 10% of its German workforce and Ford reducing 1,000 jobs at an EV plant in Cologne. VW is also facing fierce competition in China and weak European demand, and has a prior agreement to cut 35,000 jobs by 2030.

In August 2025, Honda's global automobile production fell to 267,005 units (87% year-on-year), the 13th consecutive monthly decline. Japan production dropped to 44,586 units (88.4% YoY), the first decline in three months, while overseas production was 222,419 units (86.7% YoY), also marking 13 straight monthly falls. Year-to-date global output reached 2.28 million units (91.7% of 2024). In contrast, Honda’s exports from Japan surged 126.9% to 7,307 units, driven by a 270.2% increase to North America. Domestic new vehicle sales in Japan declined 8% to 301,221 units.

On October 16, 2025, BMW reported that parts of its supplier network are affected by a trade and intellectual property dispute involving chipmaker Nexperia, which faces export restrictions from the U.S. and China amid trade tensions. BMW stated production continues as planned and is monitoring suppliers. Mercedes-Benz is also monitoring; Volkswagen said its production is unaffected. Nexperia, a major maker of basic auto chips, announced it seeks talks over the restrictions and has a new interim CEO after its former CEO was removed by a Dutch court following U.S. pressure. The Dutch government took control of Nexperia, citing concerns about technology transfer to its Chinese parent. Nexperia’s main manufacturing is in Hamburg, but most chips are packaged in China.

On October 17, 2025, the European auto association ACEA warned that European carmakers face significant production disruption unless a dispute over chipmaker Nexperia between China and the Dutch government is swiftly resolved. Nexperia notified suppliers last week it could no longer guarantee chip deliveries. The Dutch government took control of Nexperia on September 30, citing technology transfer risks to Chinese parent Wingtech, which the U.S. placed on its entity list in December. On October 4, China’s commerce ministry prohibited Nexperia China from exporting specific finished components. Most Nexperia chips, though not sophisticated, are assembled in China and needed in large volumes. The dispute threatens production stoppages.

Ford slashed its F-150 Lightning plant workforce in Dearborn to one-third of 2,100 employees, transferring or offering early retirement due to plummeting EV demand. A Sept. 16 fire at Novelis' Oswego mill, which supplies 40% of U.S. automotive aluminum, halted operations until early 2026, forcing Ford to prioritize gasoline F-series trucks and idle EV production. The crisis could cost Ford $500 million to $1 billion in EBIT, disrupt Super Duty output, and expose supply chain vulnerabilities. Ford's stock dropped 10% since the fire, as analysts warn of extended wait times and broader economic risks.

On October 21, 2025, GM Canada announced it is ending production of the BrightDrop electric delivery van at the Cami plant in Ingersoll, citing poor sales (about 2,000 units sold in 2024). The decision affects approximately 600 workers scheduled to return next month and clouds the plant’s future. Union members were blindsided. Industry analysts say the plant’s fate depends on securing a new vehicle model, which is unlikely amid the Canada-U.S. trade war and upcoming CUSMA renewal. GM is not moving production elsewhere and is evaluating options. Federal and Ontario leaders pledged to push for new production at the plant.

On October 14, 2025, the Netherlands invoked its Goods Availability Act to intervene in Chinese-owned Nexperia, citing economic security. In retaliation, China barred Nexperia's China arm from exporting certain chips. On October 21, GM CEO Mary Barra warned of potential production disruptions. Volkswagen cautioned of possible short-term production outages. The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association warned Nexperia chip stocks may last only weeks. The German VDA noted Nexperia informed automakers on October 10 it could not guarantee supplies. Honda is assessing impacts. A Japanese distributor reported a fivefold surge in orders for alternative chips amid anxiety over supply chain disruption.
On October 27, 2025, the King is scheduled to attend the dedication ceremony for the United Kingdom's first memorial honoring LGBT armed forces personnel.

On October 30, 2025, global automakers brace for production disruptions due to a chip shortage from Dutch supplier Nexperia, owned by China's Wingtech. The Dutch government took control of Nexperia after U.S. security concerns; China responded by blocking exports of its finished products. Honda reduced production. Volkswagen has until next week before supplies impact output. Stellantis operates a "war room" monitoring the situation daily. The shortage affects legacy semiconductors for basic functions like windshield wipers. ACEA warns assembly lines may stop within days. Companies seek alternative sources and open-market purchases. A U.S.-China leaders' meeting this week yielded no resolution.

Germany's Volkswagen announced on Wednesday (Nov 5, 2025) it will develop an in-house assisted driving chip for its China business via a joint venture between its software arm CARIAD and Chinese tech firm Horizon Robotics. This is the automaker's first such chip. The move aims to recover from sagging sales amid rising local brands and to insulate against global semiconductor trade tensions, especially US-China export controls. Smart driving is a key battleground in China. CEO Ralf Brandstatter cited the "In China, for China" strategy moving beyond localized production to mastering core technologies. CEO Oliver Blume said it takes control of a key technology. The chip is expected in 3–5 years, with current focus on China, though technological achievements may later feed back globally.

BMW reported rising profitability in Q3 2025, with an operating profit margin of 5.2% (up from 2.3% a year earlier) and net profit of €1.7 billion, rebounding from a recall-hit 2024. Shares jumped 6.8% in Frankfurt. CEO Oliver Zipse cited resilience despite tariffs from the US and EU on EVs made in China, and a slowing Chinese market. BMW's US deliveries rose ~25% year-on-year, offsetting slight declines in China. The company cut its 2025 outlook in October due to tariff costs and China risks. R&D spending fell significantly from 2024. Chip supply was "going well" but remains "volatile." Positive signals followed China's easing of its export ban on Nexperia semiconductors, which had threatened European production.

On November 7, Honda reported a 37% profit decline for the first fiscal half through September, attributing the drop to US President Donald Trump’s tariffs, which erased 164 billion yen ($1.1bn) in operating profit, and unfavorable currency rates. Sales fell 1.5% to 10.6 trillion yen ($69bn). Honda lowered its fiscal-year profit forecast to 300 billion yen ($2bn). A chip shortage after the Dutch government took control of Nexperia (owned by Wingtech Technology) led China to briefly block chip shipments. Since October 27-28, Honda halted production at its Celaya, Mexico plant and adjusted North American output due to supply disruptions, with no restoration date given. Motorcycle sales hit a record 10.7 million units.

Volkswagen's China chief confirmed that carmakers have received initial chip deliveries from Nexperia after a supply outage. The Dutch government seized Nexperia on September 30 due to the U.S.-China trade war, and China blocked exports from October 4, causing shortages. Under a U.S.-China agreement, Nexperia will not face U.S. export restrictions for one year, and China will grant short-term special permits case-by-case. Volkswagen’s China production is currently unaffected, but the sustainability of supply depends on U.S.-China relations, creating ongoing uncertainty.

On November 10, 2025, a New York man was charged with striking a Harford officer during a police chase. The suspect was held without bail. The incident involved a vehicle pursuit, but no details about the vehicle make, model, or any automaker supply-chain signals were reported. The article contained no further information on production, policy, or sentiment relevant to mid-size gas vehicles.

Honda cut its full-year operating profit outlook by a fifth on November 7, 2025, citing a chip shortage from Netherlands-based Nexperia and a ¥385 billion hit from US tariffs. The Japanese automaker now expects to sell 925,000 vehicles in Asia including China, down from 1.09 million. It faces intensifying competition from Chinese EV makers like BYD in Southeast Asia, where retail sales plunged nearly 30% in Indonesia and 18% in Malaysia. Honda has no new models planned for the region beyond the City compact sedan. Its automotive division reported an operating loss for the third straight quarter, while the motorcycle division delivered record profits. Honda will make India a production base for one planned electric car.

On November 12, 2025, Ford CEO Jim Farley advised aspiring executives to aim for chief supply chain officer (CSCO) roles, stating they offer greater impact than CEO. Farley noted that supply chain leaders must master technology and geopolitics, citing Apple CEO Tim Cook and GM CEO Mary Barra as examples with supply chain backgrounds. His comments come amid industry supply chain disruptions from Trump administration tariffs, costing Ford ~$1 billion and GM $3.5-4.5 billion this year. He also warned of U.S. over-reliance on foreign rare earths, after China imposed export restrictions earlier in 2025, causing auto industry chaos. Farley emphasized the need for vocational training and expressed concern over U.S. manufacturing competitiveness.

Ford employees on LinkedIn leaked that they are working on a "Gen 2 F-150 Lightning," indicating a second-generation electric truck. The new Lightning would join the next-generation F-150 lineup in late 2027 or 2028. Current production is paused due to an aluminum supplier fire, expected offline until Q1 2026; Lightning production may not restart until mid-2026. Ford CEO Jim Farley noted demand was lower than expected, with 23,034 units sold through October 2025. Executives have had active discussions about ending Lightning production, and competitor Ram canceled its electric truck in favor of a range-extender model.

On November 20, 2025, FOX45 reported that demands are growing for an investigation into Harford County Schools’ hiring of an accused felon. No additional details about the individual, the hiring process, or the nature of the accusations were provided in the article.

On November 24, 2025, German automakers Volkswagen, BMW, and Mercedes-Benz are accelerating efforts to reduce China dependence after the Nexperia crisis. Beijing’s export restrictions disrupted chip supplies, eroding Honda’s profits and forcing Bosch to scale back production. Automakers formed internal task forces; CLEPA and executives instructed suppliers to find non-Chinese semiconductor and raw-material alternatives. Analysts estimate replacing China’s chip and rare-earth dominance will take 3–7 years; lithium supply substitution could take decades. German carmakers invested EUR4.2 billion in China in 2023–2024, yet their market share fell from 25% (2021) to 10% (2025) due to domestic EV competition and weaker purchasing power. EU pressures to reduce China reliance clash with costly EV transitions and weak demand, while Chinese manufacturers expand in Europe.

On December 2, 2025, a Maryland lawmaker introduced a bill to prohibit individuals charged with a felony from working in Maryland schools. The proposed legislation targets teachers with pending felony charges, aiming to prevent their employment in educational settings. No further details on the bill's provisions or the lawmaker's identity were provided.

On December 3, 2025, Ford and Hyundai reported marginal US sales declines for November, driven by a steep drop in electric vehicle sales after President Trump's tax bill ended the $7,500 EV tax credit in October. Ford’s EV sales (Mustang Mach-E, F-150 Lightning) fell 61% to 4,247 vehicles, partly due to a fire at a key aluminum supplier plant. Overall Ford sales slipped nearly 1% to 164,925. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 and 6 each fell over 55%; total sales dropped 2%. Hyundai CEO Randy Parker noted a sharp decline after the credit expiration and a 42% surge in hybrid sales. Meanwhile, Kia posted a 2.7% gain, and Honda sales fell 15% due to semiconductor shortages.

Volkswagen Group plans to invest 160 billion euros ($186 billion) through 2030, CEO Oliver Blume announced, reflecting belt-tightening as the automaker faces crisis in China and the U.S. due to tariffs and fierce competition, which has hurt profits at Porsche. The total is down from previous five-year plans; 2024 was the peak. Focus is on Germany and Europe in products and infrastructure. Porsche will extend savings-program talks into 2026 and has rolled back its EV strategy. A potential U.S. Audi plant depends on Washington's financial support. Porsche is not expected to grow in China, but localizing wider-group production and a tailor-made Porsche model for China are possible. Blume’s CEO contract extension to 2030 signals support from major investors, though shareholders have suffered losses since Porsche’s IPO.

On December 9, 2025, JPMorgan Chase announced an advisory council for its $1.5 trillion Security and Resilience Initiative (SRI). The council, chaired by Jamie Dimon, includes Ford CEO Jim Farley, Jeff Bezos, Michael Dell, and national security experts. Farley’s inclusion signals focus on automaker supply-chain vulnerabilities; he has publicly warned about U.S. dependence on China for chips and rare earths, citing strategic vulnerability. In October, he told investors that a China-caused chip shortage threatened Ford. The SRI will invest up to $10 billion in equity and venture capital over 10 years to boost U.S. national security and economic resiliency. The council also includes Berkshire Hathaway’s Todd Combs, who will lead the SRI investment group starting January 2026.

On December 11, Ford confirmed that its Chinese rare-earth magnet suppliers were among the first to receive new streamlined export licenses from Beijing, issued after Presidents Xi and Trump met in South Korea. The "general licenses" allow larger shipments under year-long permits, reducing shortages that followed China’s April export controls. Ford is the first foreign customer to acknowledge supplier approvals under the system. Germany's Foreign Minister noted its automakers were excluded, with Volkswagen calling supply stable and BMW monitoring the issue. China’s rare-earth exports rose in November. Ford urged continued U.S.-China collaboration to fully resolve supply-chain issues.

On 2025-12-17, crowds lined streets to mourn a British soldier killed in Ukraine. Mourners gathered to pay respects, reflecting public grief over the soldier's death in the ongoing conflict. The event highlights the human toll of the war and community response to a fallen service member. No further details about the soldier or circumstances are provided in the article.

Honda will pause vehicle production at several plants in Japan (5–6 January) and in China (29 December–2 January) due to the ongoing global semiconductor shortage. In Japan, specific plants have not been identified. In China, all three factories of Guangqi Honda Automobile, a joint venture with Guangzhou Automobile Group, will shut. The fresh suspension follows previous disruption despite easing supply constraints. China had blocked exports from Nexperia, a chipmaker owned by Wingtech Technology, affecting automotive control components; export curbs were dropped in early November. Honda has revised its 2025 sales outlook down to 3.34 million units from 3.62 million and previously scaled back North American operations due to limited chip supply.

On 2026-01-10, Honda announced plans to diversify semiconductor procurement from suppliers both in and outside Japan. The automaker aims to reduce dependency on China and buffer against future chip shortages. A previous shortage late last year caused expected operating profit losses of hundreds of millions of dollars. This move targets greater supply chain resilience for its mid-size gas vehicles (HS4 8703).

On January 21, 2026, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said his government’s fall 2025 policy—a $470 million HST break for first-time homebuyers on new homes up to $1 million—had “didn’t move the needle” as he had predicted. Ford suggested expanding the tax break to all new home buyers to revive the housing sector and boost the economy amid the U.S. trade war. Housing starts in Ontario fell to 62,561 in 2025, far below the 150,000 target. Development industry sources estimated a full waiver would cost $2 billion. Ford also linked the housing crisis to the struggling auto sector.

On February 10, 2026, Honda Motor Co. reported ¥267.1 billion ($1.7 billion) in one-time EV-related expenses, including losses and asset write-offs in the U.S., plus a ¥279.5 billion hit from U.S. import duties. The automaker cited slowing EV growth, protectionist trade policies, heightened supply chain risks (rare earths, memory parts), and intense global competition as headwinds necessitating a fundamental strategy reassessment. Honda warned the planned EV transition in North America is faltering, echoing industry warnings of an "EV winter." Despite a ¥166.4 billion operating loss in automobiles, record motorcycle sales (16.4 million units) boosted overall profit. Third-quarter operating income of ¥153.4 billion beat estimates, and Honda maintained its full-year profit outlook. The company raised net sales guidance to ¥21.1 trillion and announced a 14% share buyback.

Ford CEO Jim Farley admitted Ford's electric vehicle (EV) rollout was mishandled, praising Tesla's efficient design after dismantling a Tesla. He cited COVID-19 as a false signal that inflated post-pandemic demand. Ford's Model e division posted a $4.8 billion EBIT loss in 2025. The company axed the F-150 Lightning in favor of an extended-range EV, and scrapped a three-row SUV. Farley acknowledged Chinese OEMs have surpassed Ford in China. Ford is developing a Universal EV platform; the first model, a Ranger-sized ute, is due in 2027 with a base price under $30,000 and Level 3 autonomous driving.

On March 6, 2026, at the F1 Australian Grand Prix in Albert Park, Aston Martin faces severe battery and power-unit issues supplied by Honda. Team principal Adrian Newey confirmed that two of four batteries brought are non-operational, leaving only two in drivers' cars. Vibration from the Honda power unit has limited running in practice and poses a risk of permanent nerve damage to drivers. Stroll managed only three laps in practice one; Alonso did not run. Mechanics worked until 4 a.m. Newey stated Honda is working on reducing vibration, but a quick fix is unlikely, undermining the team's competitiveness.

On March 13, 2026, Honda announced a $15.7 billion writedown of its EV business, restructuring primarily in the U.S. and writing down some Chinese operations. The automaker will report its first annual loss in nearly 70 years as a listed company. It canceled three planned U.S. battery-powered models (Saloon, Honda 0 SUV, Acura RSX) after President Trump ended EV subsidies, causing demand to crater. Honda will pivot to hybrids in the U.S. and strengthen India operations. In China, Honda sold only 17,000 EVs last year (2.5% of sales), citing inability to keep up with newer manufacturers' software and development speed, raising long-term competitiveness concerns. Cash outflows of up to 1.7 trillion yen are expected from supplier compensation.

On 2026-03-16, Honda announced the cancellation of three new EV model launches and a total $15.7bn hit. Of this, $8.1bn will be taken in the current FY ending this month, leading to a $4.3bn loss—the company’s first in 69 years. Another $7.5bn will be taken in FY ending March 2027. CEO Toshihiro Mibe acknowledged the industry transition, stating the company had failed to flexibly revise strategy amid changing market conditions and policy trends. Honda attributed the setbacks to shifts in hybrid categories, US tariffs, Chinese competition, and new EV market entrants.

Volkswagen China CTO Thomas Ulbrich said the automaker is pivoting from Nvidia to local chip partners Horizon Robotics and Xpeng for driver-assist EVs. Production of the ID. UNYX 08, VW’s first all-electric SUV using Xpeng’s Turing chip, began March 13, 2026, in Hefei; deliveries in China start by end of June. The vehicle features L2 driver-assist, with L3 expected in ~2 years. VW plans 20 new battery/hybrid models in China in 2026 and 50 by 2030, including 30 EVs. Despite a 53% profit drop and 8% China sales decline, VW is accelerating production. China’s January–February exports beat expectations, and retail sales rose 2.8% year-over-year.

On March 20, 2026, Ford’s stock had fallen over 20% from 2026 highs, pushing its dividend yield above 5%. Ford pays a quarterly dividend of $0.15, unchanged since July 2022, and targets returning 40–50% of annual free cash flow to shareholders. It did not announce a special dividend this year, after paying supplemental dividends in prior years. Free cash flow tumbled to $3.5 billion in 2025 from $6.7 billion in 2024, attributed to President Trump’s tariffs and supply chain issues after a fire at a key supplier. For 2026, Ford guided adjusted free cash flow between $5–6 billion. Analysts give a consensus “Hold,” but Bank of America issued a “Buy” rating with a $17 target. Ford continues to face severe recall issues, with 153 recalls covering 12.9 million vehicles in 2025, the highest for any automaker.

Sony and Honda discontinued development of their AFEELA electric vehicle line on March 25, 2026, and will refund reservation fees. The Sony Honda Mobility (SHM) joint venture cited Honda’s March 12 EV strategy reassessment, which prevents Honda from providing originally planned technologies and assets, leaving no viable path to market. AFEELA had been promoted as recently as March 18 and had appeared at CES 2023, 2024, and 2026. The discontinuation follows rising tech costs driven by memory and chip shortages linked to AI investments. SHM remains in business.

Honda posted its first-ever loss in 70+ years for fiscal year ended March 2026, with EV-related losses of ¥1.579 trillion ($10 billion) and an operating loss of ¥414.3 billion ($2.625 billion). However, guidance for fiscal March 2027 topped estimates, forecasting ¥500 billion operating profit despite ¥500 billion in EV losses, sending ADR shares up over 5%. Honda will roll out 15 new hybrid models by 2030, primarily in North America, and dropped plans for a Canada EV battery supply chain. It scrapped its 2040 combustion-free target, aiming for carbon neutrality by 2050. Tariff expenses for the past year totaled ¥346.9 billion ($2.2 billion).

On October 13, 2025, Chinese semiconductor firm Wingtech announced it will seek help from Beijing government departments after Dutch authorities invoked the Goods Availability Act in late September to take control of Wingtech’s European subsidiary Nexperia. The Dutch government cited national security concerns, “serious governance shortcomings,” and threats to crucial technological knowledge in Europe. While Nexperia continues regular production, its decisions can be blocked or reversed. Wingtech vowed to protect its interests, is discussing legal remedies with international law firms, and is proactively engaging Chinese government departments. Nexperia, bought by Wingtech in 2018, makes chips for cars and refrigerators. Semiconductors remain a key China-West battleground; Wingtech was placed on a U.S. entity list in December 2024.

On October 14, 2025, the China Semiconductor Industry Association denounced Dutch government intervention in Nexperia, a Dutch subsidiary of Chinese firm Wingtech. The association opposed discriminatory restrictions under the "national security" pretext, warning they harm the global semiconductor ecosystem. Wingtech stated the move reflects geopolitical bias, violates EU trade rules, and followed a Dutch order under the "Availability of Goods Act" and legal actions against management. Wingtech noted Nexperia’s revenue peaked at 2.36 billion euros in 2022 and achieved zero-debt by October 2024. The company demanded the order be revoked. China’s foreign ministry also condemned politicizing economic issues.

On October 24, 2025, Wingtech Technology, Nexperia’s Chinese parent, warned the Dutch government that failing to regain control of its seized chipmaking unit by end-2025 would pressure revenue, profit, and cash flow. The Dutch government seized Nexperia last month after mounting US pressure following Wingtech’s 2024 Entity List placement, citing concerns over Nexperia’s independence and removing its Chinese CEO. Although Wingtech reported a 12.2% YoY Q3 semiconductor revenue rise, long-term growth is now in doubt. The dispute has fueled supply-chain stability worries ahead of US-China trade talks, with China’s commerce minister warning of serious global effects. The Dutch government stated it remains in contact with Chinese authorities seeking a constructive solution.

On October 30, 2025, Toyota Motor CEO Koji Sato stated at the Japan Mobility Show in Tokyo that the automaker does not face an immediate chip shortage following China's export curbs on Dutch semiconductor firm Nexperia. However, he acknowledged potential production risks if restrictions persist. His comments follow Dutch government seizure of Nexperia, citing national security risks linked to its Chinese parent Wingtech, and Beijing's retaliatory export restrictions. Sato noted that Japanese manufacturers are working to standardize older semiconductors to avoid a repeat of pandemic-era shortages, while Toyota closely monitors supply chains.

On November 4, 2025, China criticized the Dutch government for failing to take sufficient steps to resolve a dispute over chipmaker Nexperia, which has led to a supply crunch for the automotive industry. China’s Ministry of Commerce urged the Netherlands to “stop interfering” in Nexperia’s internal affairs and seek a constructive solution, according to a statement on Bloomberg Terminal. The dispute has disrupted supply chains for doped electronic materials (HS4 3818), impacting automakers.

The Dutch government suspended its state intervention at chipmaker Nexperia on November 19, 2025, citing constructive talks with China over a dispute that had caused shortages of automotive chips. The Netherlands had taken control of Nexperia on September 30 to prevent its former CEO from moving operations to China. In response, China halted exports of Nexperia's finished products on October 4, later relaxing the measure. Dutch Economy Minister Vincent Karremans called the suspension a gesture of goodwill, expressing optimism about Chinese steps to ensure chip supply to Europe. Nexperia is a major supplier of basic computer chips to car manufacturers; the dispute threatened automotive supply chains, leading to production slowdowns and halts.

On November 20, 2025, the Netherlands paused an order related to Nexperia, a producer of doped electronic materials (HS4 3818), following talks with China. The decision helped ease auto-chip supply-chain strain. However, the pause did not resolve underlying structural questions regarding the order.

On September 30, 2025, the Netherlands’ Ministry of Economic Affairs seized control of chipmaker Nexperia, citing national security concerns and invoking the 1952 Goods Availability Act. The order prohibited Nexperia from relocating company assets without explicit Dutch government permission for one year. The seizure sparked a clash between Nexperia’s head office in Nijmegen and its mainland China unit, which vowed to continue operations independently and fulfill orders.

In late September 2025, the Dutch government seized control of Netherlands-based chipmaker Nexperia, citing concerns over technology transfer to its Chinese owner Wingtech. China retaliated by halting exports of finished Nexperia chips packaged at a plant in the Pearl River Delta. The factory became a global choke point for automotive chips, reigniting supply-chain disruptions. Automakers had vowed to strengthen supply lines after COVID-19 disruptions in 2020 and a 2021 Japanese factory fire, but the Nexperia crisis exposed a blind spot: low-tech chips as geopolitical leverage. “No one prepared for geopolitical disruption, and they’re still not prepared,” said Seraph Consulting CEO Ambrose Conroy.

On November 27, 2025, Nexperia's parent company Wingtech Technology publicly accused the Dutch headquarters of deception and obstruction, escalating a corporate conflict. The Dutch office had suspended wafer shipments and cut Chinese employees from IT systems. Wingtech seeks restoration of lawful control, arguing it is prerequisite for supply-chain stability. The Dutch office plans a $300 million Malaysian expansion, which Nexperia China claims would shift output overseas. Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao raised the issue in video conferences with German and EU trade officials, who urged resumption of internal talks. The standoff over governance, operational control, and production geography threatens to disrupt automotive and industrial supply chains.

On November 27, 2025, Wingtech Technology publicly accused Nexperia’s Dutch headquarters of deception and obstruction, deepening a conflict that disrupted wafer flows. Nexperia Netherlands had suspended wafer shipments and cut Chinese employees from IT systems, while proposing a $300 million Malaysian expansion that Nexperia China said would sideline its Dongguan facility. Despite the rift, Nexperia China shipped 7.4 billion components to over 500 customers since October. Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao raised the issue with German and EU trade officials, who agreed that internal talks should resume promptly for a long-term solution.

On December 2, 2025, Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Vincent Karremans canceled a planned December visit to China, citing scheduling differences. He informed parliament he remains ready to travel on short notice for talks over chipmaker Nexperia, whose state seizure on September 30 prompted Chinese retaliatory export restrictions, disrupting automotive supply chains. Karremans published a timeline showing he learned on September 18 that Nexperia’s former management had advanced plans to move operations to China, posing an economic security threat. He decided to intervene on September 25, notifying Britain, Germany, the U.S., and China only after the action. Nexperia’s parent Wingtech has appealed the intervention and a court ruling suspending its former CEO.

Caretaker economic affairs minister Vincent Karremans cancelled the December 9 trade mission to China, citing scheduling conflicts as Chinese ministers attend the Central Economic Work Conference and stating that a ministerial meeting would be premature while diplomatic talks continue. The dispute began in September when Karremans placed chipmaker Nexperia under state supervision over fears its Chinese owner would transfer intellectual property from Nijmegen to China. Beijing retaliated with an export ban on Nexperia chips, causing weeks of supply uncertainty for carmakers. After a November delegation to ease tensions, Karremans suspended restrictions, saying he no longer sees an immediate risk of production transfer. He faces a parliamentary debate on Thursday. The business delegation will proceed without him.

On December 4, 2025, the dispute involving Nexperia escalated. The Dutch minister canceled a planned visit to China, and Beijing responded by spotlighting the former chair of Wingtech. The event signals rising tensions around Nexperia, a semiconductor firm, amid trade and policy friction.

On September 30, Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Vincent Karremans seized control of Nexperia, a Dutch subsidiary of China's Wingtech, to prevent relocation of secrets and production to China. He did not inform European, U.S., or Chinese governments beforehand. On October 4, China retaliated by blocking Nexperia's chip exports, causing a supply shock for European carmakers. Both governments later eased interventions, but internal conflict emerged: Nexperia's Chinese packaging arm declared independence and seeks Chinese wafers, while the European arm halted wafer shipments to China due to nonpayment. Stockpiles are dwindling, and car industry fears renewed shortages. Karremans defended his lone-wolf approach in a parliamentary debate, saying it prevented European dependency on non-European legacy chip vendors.

On December 8, 2025, China’s Vice-Minister of Commerce Ling Ji pressed German automotive industry leaders in separate video meetings to use their influence with the European Commission to resolve disputes over EU anti-subsidy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and the Nexperia semiconductor issue. Ling spoke with VDA president Hildegard Mueller and Mercedes-Benz chairman Ola Kallenius. Mueller reiterated the VDA’s opposition to the tariffs and expressed hope for resolving Nexperia’s internal disputes through dialogue. She pointed to rare earth restrictions and the Nexperia saga as areas needing long-term supply-chain solutions.

On 2025-12-09, Nexperia, a Dutch semiconductor firm, was portrayed as a casualty of the US-China trade war. The Dutch government’s compliance with US demands and defiance toward China left it exposed. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth warned at the Reagan National Defense Forum that model allies would receive favor, while those failing to contribute faced consequences. When Washington and Beijing agreed to a one-year trade truce, the Netherlands was left “holding the bag” over Nexperia, highlighting how European states became pawns in US President Donald Trump’s America-first strategy.
